gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the $989.99 price on ChatGPT's 'best value 4K' Nebula Cosmos 4K SE card matches Amazon's Renewed listing; a new unit costs $1,099.99 on Amazon and $1,299.99 at Nebula, so a new Nebula X1 at $1,899.00 on Amazon is only $799 more, and ProjectorCentral measured the X1 at 2,588 ANSI lumens in Standard mode.
standout_why: I compared against the Wirecutter best-projectors page (cited, updated 2026-10-05) and the ProjectorCentral X1 review (result 10). Wirecutter prices the Mars 3 ($900) and Mars 3 Air ($520) and has their measured brightness and battery times. It does not cover the Cosmos 4K SE or the Nebula X1 at all, and it says nothing about new versus renewed pricing. ProjectorCentral has the X1's measured lumens but no Cosmos comparison and no current price. Three cited pages showed me no pick content: the RTINGS outdoor list (JS-rendered, only a sidebar came back), Yahoo Tech (HTTP 403) and What Hi-Fi (truncated). I did not open Forbes, and geekchamp timed out. So I can't rule out that those pages mention the Cosmos 4K SE, but none of them could show that ChatGPT's $989.99 is a Renewed price, because that comes from today's listing.
decides: Comparing new prices changes the order of the picks. ChatGPT made the Cosmos 4K SE its 'best value 4K' at $989.99, but new it costs $1,099.99 on Amazon and $1,299.99 at Nebula. That leaves a small gap to the X1 at $1,899.00 on Amazon. ProjectorCentral measured the X1 at 2,588 lm, against the Cosmos's 1,800 lm rating; I found no measured figure for the Cosmos. For a 120–150-inch screen with a power outlet, the X1 at Amazon's price is the pick, and it beats the X1's own $2,999.00 on Nebula's store. Without an outlet the Mars 3 stays the pick at $899.99 on Amazon: Wirecutter measured just over 800 lumens and about 2 hours at 100% brightness, so it suits screens around 100 inches.
